Strengthen Your Express.js API Security with Helmet + CORS + Rate Limiter!
Hey everyone! Today I’m gonna share some quick tips on beefing up the security of our Express.js API using a pretty straightforward approach with Helmet + CORS + Rate Limiter. As developers, paying attention to API security is super important for a few key reasons:
1.
Sensitive Data Protection: APIs often access and process sensitive data, like user personal info or financial data. Without proper security, this data is vulnerable to theft or misuse.
2.
Preventing Unauthorized Access: With solid API security, you can ensure that only authorized users or systems can access specific data or functionality.
3.
Maintaining System Integrity: An insecure API can be an entry point for attackers to damage or modify your system. This could lead to data corruption or even service disruptions.
4.
Preventing API Abuse: DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks are a technique where attackers flood the API with excessive requests to cripple the system. Implementing rate limiting helps ensure system resources are shared fairly and no single user or client abuses the API with too many requests in a short time.
5.
User Trust: Users expect their data to be safe. A vulnerable API can damage your company’s reputation and erode user trust in the services offered.
Pretty crucial, right, to secure the APIs we build after reading those reasons? Alright, no more chit-chat—let’s dive straight into implementing Helmet + CORS + Rate Limiter to secure our Express.js API!
1. Sample Project
Here, I’ll create a sample Express.js project using TypeScript for this post. Feel free to skip this section if you want to implement Helmet + CORS + Rate Limiter in your own personal projects.
import express, { Request, Response } from 'express'; import bodyParser from 'body-parser'; import { v4 as uuidv4 } from 'uuid'; const app = express(); app.use( bodyParser.json() ); type Todo = { id: string; task: string; completed: boolean; }; let todos: Todo[] = []; app.get('/api/todos', (req: Request, res: Response) => { res.json(todos); }); app.post('/api/todos', (req: Request, res: Response) => { const newTodo: Todo = { id: uuidv4(), task: req.body.task, completed: false, }; todos.push(newTodo); res.status(201).json(newTodo); }); app.put('/api/todos/:id', (req: Request, res: Response) => { const updatedTodo = todos.find(todo => todo.id === req.params.id); if (!updatedTodo) { res.status(404).send("Todo not found"); return; } updatedTodo.task = req.body.task; if (req.body.completed !== undefined) { updatedTodo.completed = req.body.completed; } res.json(updatedTodo); }); app.delete('/api/todos/:id', (req: Request, res: Response) => { const todo = todos.find(todo => todo.id === req.params.id); if (!todo) { res.status(404).send("Todo not found"); return; } todos = todos.filter(todo => todo.id !== req.params.id); res.status(200).send("Success - Todo deleted"); }); const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000; app.listen(PORT, () => { console.log(`Server running on port ${PORT}`); });
The code above is a simple CRUD To Do project with zero security measures applied. You can copy-paste it for practice.
2. CORS Installation + Implementation
Before we get into installation and implementation, let me quickly explain what CORS is. CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing—it’s a security mechanism implemented by web browsers to allow or restrict HTTP requests from one domain (origin) to another.
For example, say your backend runs on http://localhost:3000 and your frontend on http://localhost:5000. Even though they’re on the same machine (localhost), different ports mean the browser sees them as different origins.
If CORS isn’t enabled on the backend, the frontend can’t make requests to it because the browser blocks them under the Same-Origin Policy. As a result, requests from frontend to backend fail, and the needed data can’t be fetched or sent.
To fix this, you need to enable CORS on the backend so it allows requests from http://localhost:5000.
Install CORS via npm with the code below.
// typescript npm install cors @types/cors // javascript npm install cors
After that, implement CORS as simply as adding cors() to app.use().
... import cors from 'cors'; ... app.use( bodyParser.json(), cors() ); ...
The CORS implementation above defaults to allowing all origins ("origin": "*"). For extra security, you can configure specific CORS options with the code below.
... // allow specific origins const corsOptions = { origin: 'http://localhost:3000', method: "GET,HEAD,PUT,PATCH,POST,DELETE", // only allow HTTP methods credentials: true, // allow credentials optionsSuccessStatus: 200, // some legacy browsers (IE11, various SmartTVs) choke on 204 }; ...
Then modify and add those options to cors() like this.
... import cors from 'cors'; ... app.use( bodyParser.json(), cors(corsOptions) ); ...
3. Helmet Installation + Implementation
Next up: installing and implementing Helmet. So what is Helmet? Simply put, it’s a package that sets up additional security headers. By default, Helmet adds these headers:
•
Content-Security-Policy: A strong set of permissions about what can happen on your pages, reducing many attack types.
•
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: Helps isolate your page’s process.
•
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: Prevents others from loading your resources cross-origin.
•
Origin-Agent-Cluster: Changes process isolation to be origin-based.
•
Referrer-Policy: Controls the Referer header.
•
Strict-Transport-Security: Tells browsers to prefer HTTPS.
•
X-Content-Type-Options: Prevents MIME sniffing.
•
X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: Controls DNS prefetching.
•
X-Download-Options: Forces downloads to be saved (IE only).
•
X-Frame-Options: Old header that reduces clickjacking risk.
•
X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies: Controls cross-domain behavior for Adobe products like Acrobat.
•
X-Powered-By: Web server info. Helmet removes this to prevent simple attacks.
•
X-XSS-Protection: Old header that tries to mitigate XSS but often worsens it, so Helmet disables it.
Install Helmet via npm with the code below.
npm install helmet
After that, implement Helmet as simply as adding helmet() to app.use().
... import helmet from 'helmet'; ... app.use( bodyParser.json(), cors(), helmet() ); ...
4. Rate Limiter Installation + Implementation
Finally, rate limiter installation and implementation. Many cloud providers offer rate limiting options in their services, but some charge extra for it.
This time, we’ll handle simple rate limiting ourselves using the express-rate-limit package.
Install express-rate-limit via npm with the code below.
npm install express-rate-limit
Then, we’ll manually set up the rate limiter we’ll use with this code.
... import rateLimit from 'express-rate-limit'; ... const limiter = rateLimit({ legacyHeaders: false, // Disable the `X-RateLimit-*` headers standardHeaders: 'draft-7', // draft-6: `RateLimit-*` headers; draft-7: combined `RateLimit` header windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, // 15 minutes limit: 100, // limit each IP to 100 requests per windowMs message: "Too many requests, please try again later", // optional message }); ...
After that, implement the rate limiter settings by simply adding limiter to app.use().
... app.use( bodyParser.json(), cors(), helmet(), limiter ); ...
Boom, super easy to strengthen our Express.js API security with those 3 packages, right? That’s it for this post—hope it’s helpful for you all, and thanks for reading!
